name: logs
title: A daily report from a log
pitch: Logs say what happened on a machine, but nobody reads ten thousand lines. Your script will count errors, find the busiest addresses and hours, and write a short report every day.

steps.do: Copy a log into a test folder: a web server access log, or `journalctl` output saved to a file.
steps.done: the file holds a few hundred lines.
steps.hint: `journalctl --since yesterday > test.log`, or `/var/log/nginx/access.log` if you run a web server.
steps.why: Logs change all the time. A copy holds still, so your counts can be checked by hand.

steps.done: you know how many lines the log has.
steps.why: Know the size of your data first: it tells you if a result later looks plausible.

steps.do: Count the errors with grep (the word error, or HTTP codes 5xx in an access log).
steps.done: the count matches what you see in the file.
steps.hint: `grep -c`, `-i` to ignore case, and a regex like `" 5[0-9][0-9] "` for the codes.
steps.why: A search is only as good as its pattern: too wide and it counts lines that aren't errors, too narrow and it misses some. Check a few matches by eye.

steps.do: Find the 10 addresses that appear the most.
steps.done: the list is sorted from the most frequent to the least.
steps.why: This pipeline (extract, sort, count, sort again) answers "what comes up most?" about any data. It's one of the most useful lines in the shell.

steps.do: Count the requests (or messages) per hour.
steps.done: you get one line per hour with a number.
steps.hint: Cut the hour out of the date field with `awk` or `cut`, then the same count as before.
steps.why: Counts over time show patterns: the night backup, the lunch rush, an attack at 3 am.

steps.done: a line from yesterday isn't counted.
steps.hint: Build today's date in the log's own format with `date +…`, and `grep` for it.
steps.why: Each log writes dates its own way. Matching their format, not yours, is the trick.

steps.do: Put it in a script that takes the log file as its argument.
steps.done: `./report.sh access.log` prints the counts, and a missing file prints a clear message.
steps.hint: `$1`, `[[ -r $1 ]]` to check you can read it, and functions to keep each count apart.
steps.why: Functions make a long script readable: each one does one count and has a name that says which.

steps.do: Make the report readable: a title, sections, and aligned columns.
steps.done: someone else understands the report without your help.
steps.why: A report is for people. Aligned numbers can be compared at a glance; ragged ones have to be read one by one.

steps.do: Run it every day with cron or a systemd timer, and save each report in a dated file.
steps.done: a new report file appears each day.
steps.hint: Redirect the output: `report.sh log > reports/$(date +%F).txt`. In crontab, % must be written \%.
steps.why: Automation is where scripts pay off. Note the cron trap: % has a special meaning in a crontab line.

steps.do: Optional: compare with yesterday's report and show what grew.
steps.done: the report says how many more (or fewer) errors there are than yesterday.
steps.hint: Keep today's numbers in a small file, read yesterday's, and subtract with `$(( ))`.
steps.why: A trend says more than a number. That's how monitoring tools decide when to wake someone up.
